📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The firm on Monday rolled out a newly introduced “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.

The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company notes.

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help customers decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.

In a recent development, the feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let owners engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces newly introduced competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.

According to recent reports, audible’s newly introduced feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.

It has been revealed that but such a feature could limit owners’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.).

Audible notes the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside upcoming personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company mentioned.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” remarked Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

#615. Where should you place your Wi-Fi router for the best internet?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (685 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Where should you place your Wi-Fi router for the best internet?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't reduce your router's capabilities by stuffing it into a cabinet in the corner of the room.
  • A weak Wi-Fi signal isn't always a sign of your router going bad or ISP issues.
  • In a recent development, the best spot for your Wi-Fi router differs depending on your building and where you want it to cover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't reduce your router's capabilities by stuffing it into a cabinet in the corner of the room.

A weak Wi-Fi signal isn't always a sign of your router going bad or ISP issues. More often than not, it's an indication of a placement problem. Wi-Fi routers broadcast signals in all directions, but the signal weakens over distance, so where you place your router affects the signal quality that reaches your devices. A router stuffed into a corner will likely send much of its signal outside the house where no one needs it. There's also the fact that other electronics can interfere, degrading signal quality simply by being too close.

In a recent development, the best spot for your Wi-Fi router differs depending on your building and where you want it to cover. For example, if you're covering an apartment, the best place for your Wi-Fi router will likely be somewhere that's central and away from electronics that weaken signals.

First, find a central and elevated spot in your home, away from sources of interference, so the router can evenly distribute signal across your space. This could be a side table, desk or even the top of a cabinet. If need be, consider making or buying a stand for the router. Next, keep the router in the open and away from corners, so the signal doesn't wastefully broadcast outside or get blocked.

In a recent development, if your house has two stories, you should move the router closer to the ceiling if it's on the ground floor, or closer to the floor if it's on the second level. Your router's antenna positioning matters too. For single floors or apartments, vertical antenna placement is best. For buildings with multiple floors, angle at least one antenna to about 30 degrees, then keep the others vertical.

Recent findings suggest that before you settle for a position, you'll need to run speed tests to make sure you've picked the best spot. Run the first test before you start adjusting your router to get an idea of its current performance. Next, run tests while you're adjusting the router's position so you can get a clear read on how each position affects your signal quality and internet speed.

According to recent reports, to get the most out of your router, you'll need to minimize interference. Keep your router away from item that interfere with Wi-Fi signals, including metal objects, thick walls (especially metal and concrete), Bluetooth devices and microwaves, which interfere with your router's 2.4GHz band.

Keep in mind that the 2.4GHz band has a longer signal range but slower speeds, while the 5GHz band has a shorter range with faster speeds. So connect devices where speed and stability matter most, like desktop PCs and gaming consoles, to the 5GHz band. Then keep devices that are far away, move a lot or don't need a ton of speed on the 2.4GHz band.

Sometimes, no matter how well you position the router, it still won't cover dead zones. This is especially true for large buildings, or those with three or more floors. In that case, you'll need a Wi-Fi booster (often called a Wi-Fi extender or repeater) or a mesh network.

The best Wi-Fi extenders boost your router's signal coverage by capturing said signal and repeating it to nearby spaces. But this usually comes at the cost of halving your bandwidth, and getting the right Wi-Fi extender placement can be tricky in large spaces. It's a good solution if you want something that's cheap and easy to set up, and don't have a large space to cover. But extenders are often a pain.

Sources indicate that top mesh systems solve the same problem and offer superior performance compared to extenders, but are more expensive. Unlike extenders, mesh systems use nodes that you place in dead zones to extend coverage while keeping everything on a single network. And tri-band systems avoid the pitfall of halving your bandwidth. Mesh systems are a better choice for larger buildings, multi-story homes, and spaces with several dead zones where a single extender isn't enough.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for customers to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has remarked that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription prepares, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the newly introduced system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:.

According to recent reports, the usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

Recent findings suggest that as you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ proposal.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:.

Recent findings suggest that the usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ initiative. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis.

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.
  • The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row.
  • Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.

The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.

Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower.

On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday.

Bitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets.

On Friday, the dollar index — which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin — reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.

Recent findings suggest that "A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia's results add to the tech selling," he noted. "The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over.".

Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, mentioned he's monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides.

"Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling," he noted. "For a recovery to hold, spot buyers need to keep showing up after the forced selling has passed.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other new capabilities for Ask Maps.

Ask Maps can now build travel itineraries that feature numbered map pins for each stop. It supports everything from shopping excursions to multi-day road trips with several stops. When used for the latter, Google Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with tips and the numbered pins that aid visualization. Intends can be shared with others and exported to Google Docs on desktop.

Once on the trip, Ask Maps will show directions and real-time details, including live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and “even what the vibe is at your next stop.” You can conversationally have Google add more stops to the itinerary.

Meanwhile, Ask Maps can now tap into your saved lists to find bookmarked places and take action. This lets you ask: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”.

Before you start directions, you’ll see familiar “Know Before You Go” tips that surface information about your route, like parking locations, car charging options, weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Fresh agentic capabilities let Ask Maps find online beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, as well as call local businesses on your behalf. For example, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me” returns a list of open slots.

Finally, Ask Maps is expanding to 30 more countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK.

Recent findings suggest that these updates are rolling out starting today on Google Maps for Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and list search are available in all 200+ Ask Maps countries. Know Before You Go in directions and appointment booking are coming first to the US.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Best Digital Photo Frames (2026): Aura, Skylight, Amazon

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital photo frames aren't new technology, but they're still one of my favorite pieces of tech to put into a home.
  • According to recent reports, best of all, you don't have to settle for just a digital photo frame anymore.
  • Here are all the best photo frames I've tried over years of testing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Digital photo frames aren't new technology, but they're still one of my favorite pieces of tech to put into a home. These devices promise something simple: a beautiful frame to display all the photos sitting on your camera roll, displayed for you to enjoy at any time.

According to recent reports, best of all, you don't have to settle for just a digital photo frame anymore. While my favorite digital photo frames from Aura excel at displaying your photos (and keeping your life subscription-free!), there's a nice variety of options if you want something that displays your pictures and does a little more, too. Want something that doubles as a family calendar or has a voice assistant to answer your questions? This guide has picks for that. Want something totally wireless? I've tested those, too.

Here are all the best photo frames I've tried over years of testing. Looking for more home gadgets? Don't miss our guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars, Best Smart Speakers, and Best Sunrise Alarm Clocks.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

I've been testing digital photo frames for almost six years now and always sing their praises. These devices are designed to look like a regular photo frame, but with a screen inside that displays whichever photos you send to it. There's always an app involved to upload images, and you can also usually send photos over email, too. Both the email option and the app let you invite other family members to the frame, so multiple people can send images. It's perfect for families living in the same house or for long-distance family members who want to share their best pictures with Grandma.

I also like that these devices are fairly intuitive and minimal. Digital photo frames simply connect to your Wi-Fi and display your photos. There are also options that can do multiple things if you want a multipurpose device in your home, but your frame doesn't have to do anything but show your photos.

In a recent development, do you have any photos on a digital device, like a smartphone, computer, or camera? Or does someone in your family have photos they could send to you or directly to the frame itself? Then yes, a digital photo frame is absolutely worth buying. If you have photos you take and want to see regularly or wish you had all your wedding photos on display instead of just the ones that fit on your wall, a digital photo frame will easily solve that for you.

It has been revealed that they're also great to purchase as a gift. I've given two different digital photo frames to my parents over the years and am at the moment helping my mother pick one out to gift my grandmother to enjoy photos in her nursing home. It's a great gift for young parents, too, who have camera rolls packed with photos of their fresh baby (or their fur baby!) and photo aficionados who will never have enough frames in their house for their work.

There's no beating Aura when it comes to digital frames, and it's the option I recommend most to everyone in my life after using Aura's frames since 2021. All of them have high-quality displays and unlimited photo storage, a combo you won't find anywhere else. Aura's frames are simple to set up, use, and share with family and friends, too. Everything is controlled with the app, so there's no laggy touchscreen to futz with—you can scroll through or heart photos using the touch bar on top and use the app to control how rapidly your photos change and other settings. My frames are shared with my husband, but I can also scroll down and see my parents’ frames that they've shared with me, all in one application.

Recent findings suggest that aura has had a lot of frame designs over the years, but it’s focused now on its mat-style frames that look fantastic in your home. These frames all have different names, but are nearly identical otherwise. The 10-inch Carver Mat ($179) is a mat version of the popular affordable Carver frame, and it sits in a landscape mode that will show vertical photos side by side. The other two are the 12-inch Aspen ($229) and 15-inch Walden ($299), which are flat on the back so that they can be mounted on a wall in either landscape or portrait mode. I've tried all three, and my personal favorite is the Walden for my home, but that's since I have one massive great room that encompasses the dining room, kitchen, and living room, and the Walden sits in a far corner but is easily visible from any point in the room. If you're working with a more normal room size, the Carver and Aspen are both great sizes, but I do like that the Aspen can be rotated to portrait or landscape orientation; the Carver will only do landscape, and can't be wall-mounted, either. It's up to you if that's worth spending more.

No matter which model you choose, the best part about the Aura frames is that they don't look like shiny computer screens nor are they haunted by the blue tinge you'll find on cheaper digital frames. Especially thanks to the mat style you'll find on these three models, they can easily pass for a real photo—until the picture changes, of course. There's really no better experience you can find in the world of digital photo frames.

Sources indicate that I've liked Skylight's photo frames well enough, but my favorite product from Skylight is its digital wall calendars. These calendars double as digital photo frames and digital wall calendars since you can set up a photo screensaver to pop up when you aren't interacting with it. The only downside is you'll have to pay a subscription fee to use the photo feature, but all of Skylight's devices have some kind of paywall associated with them.

In a recent development, the Skylight Calendar 2 is the newest of its three calendar models, but feels like the Goldilocks option with its 15-inch screen that's a good size for kitchen countertops or to mount on the wall, faster performance compared to older models, a more reasonable price point (the Skylight Calendar Max has a wild price tag), and interchangeable snap frames so you can adjust the look of your device to match your current home aesthetic. It's a great device that has made it easy to peek at my family's calendar whenever I want, and my son uses the Skylight Buddy in his room to track his own daily routine, but I could also teach him to just use the Calendar 2 for it instead. While the screen isn't as matte as the Aura frames, photos still look great on this screen, and the uploader tool is easy to use.

It has been revealed that if you like the idea of Skylight but don't want a subscription to have the photo feature (and don't mind missing out on the calendar and chores), you can get the Skylight Frame 2 ($190). There's still a subscription option for that model for certain features, like making albums and having a cloud backup, but you don't need it to have the basic digital photo frame experience. The Frame-only subscription is cheaper than the calendar one—$39 a year for Frame Plus versus $79 a year for Calendar Plus—but you get less, since the Calendar Plus subscription includes meal planning, an AI uploading tool, and more. I like Skylight's options a lot, especially with the newly introduced calendar-based ecosystem, but the subscription fee is the main downside. But you can get a lot more features out of your device.

Industry observers note that I didn't expect to like Amazon's newly introduced Alexa Photo Frame. I thought it would be gimmicky and frustrating to use, especially as someone who's hated Amazon's photo uploader tool in the past for its smart displays. But I found myself surprisingly pleased not only with the frame itself, but even the smart speaker experience built into it. It does help that I already have an Amazon Prime subscription, which you'll want to have unlimited photo storage and to get Alexa+ voice access on the device.

Industry observers note that what helps is that the Alexa Photo Frame uses the Amazon Photos app. It's similar to the Google Photos app in that it wants to back up all your photos for you from your phone, and it also connects to and controls this new digital photo frame. (I can also control which photos are added to my other Alexa smart displays through the app under the devices tab, so it's not exclusive to the Alexa Photo Frame.) I uploaded a handful of photos to the frame and was impressed with how nice the experience looked. The display looked a little more matte than my Skylight Calendar 2 when I put them side by side, and it has a mat-style frame that reminds me of the Aura frames. The Alexa Photo Frame has only a 10.1-inch screen, and no option to rotate it between landscape or portrait; the included stand puts it into landscape mode only, making it much like the Aura Carver Mat in specs and design. It does not, however, have a Photo Match option, so the paired vertical photos can look a bit random.

The Alexa Photo Frame also costs more than the Carver, since it comes with an extra bonus: Amazon's AI-powered voice assistant, Alexa+. I was impressed that even though this device is flat enough to be wall-mounted, Alexa's voice still sounded full and clear without any tinny quality, and music actually sounded pretty good too. I'd prefer a real speaker, but if you wanted one device for just photos and simple questions without any other screen clutter, this is a good option. This device is best for Prime owners who will get Alexa+ for free and free photo storage to boot.

Sources indicate that aura came out with the first Aura Ink frame last fall, and I was impressed by its unique color E Ink screen and fully wireless experience that made it a frame I was actually willing to mount on my wall. As of this week, Aura has a new addition to its cordless Ink lineup: the Ink 10-inch, which has a smaller screen, expanded color palette, and 200 pixels-per-inch resolution.

Like the Aura frames I recommend throughout this story, the Aura Ink 10-inch has unlimited storage and is run through Aura's clean, intuitive app that has no subscription tiers. But the Ink 10-inch (and the larger Ink 13-inch) use an E Ink screen like a color e-reader does to run on a battery, so you can place the frame anywhere without needing to constantly plug it in. While the Ink 10-inch is smaller, it has a latest nine-color e-paper display that adds off-white, mustard yellow, and orange to its color wheel. It still has a newspaper-like look to it, and Aura's technology will run photos through its algorithm to convert them onto the e-paper screen.

The Aura Ink defaults to only show one photo a day to preserve battery life and because the transition to change photos takes longer than on a standard screen. But the Ink 10-inch does have a prettier, melt-like transition effect instead of the flashing that the Ink 13-inch does when it switches photos overnight. There's also a subtle front light in both the Ink 10-inch and Ink 13-inch, but it looks best when hit with natural light to help illuminate it. It's a great option if you want something that won't have a cord and don't mind a newspaper-like look. It looks more realistic than other frames with this e-paper screen; friends of mine have genuinely been shocked when I tell them it's a digital frame.

The Aura Carver has been around for a while, and it's still a great frame. The 10-inch frame is one of the best cheap frames you can find, pairing Aura's fantastic experience (a great app! unlimited storage!) with a smaller, landscape-only option. While it does have a slimmer aspect ratio of 16:10, landscape photos still look good, and you can toggle on Photo Match in the settings to have the frame “match” to similar portrait orientation photos together to fill the screen. It'll often match by event or match two photos of the same person together.

The Aura Carver also has the Carver Mat ($179) version for a little higher price tag that matches the aesthetic of the other mat versions and is included as part of our top pick. But if you're looking for the cheapest option while still getting the great experience Aura offers, the base Aura Carver is the cheapest you'll find. It's also often on sale during events like Black Friday, so keep an eye out.

Nixplay Classic 10.1-Inch Frame for $190: Nixplay is semi-comparable to Aura, with a range of digital photo frames that's been around for years. But you will be hit with a subscription fee if you want more than 500 MB of photos on your device—Nixplay Lite costs $20 a year for 100 GB, while Nixplay Plus costs $30 for unlimited photo storage. You'll get other features, too, like ability to add longer video clips and connect to more frames, but the storage aspect is the part you'll run into after using this frame for a long time. I tested the Classic 10.1" Frame that's been around for a while, and while it's easy and intuitive to use, I found the settings slow to update from changes I make in the app, and I don't like the distracting transitions the frame will use by default. It also has a surprising amount of border for vertical photos in portrait mode. It's still a fine frame overall, especially if you're able to manage your storage usage, but it remains only an honorable mention for me still. Plus, you can get the Aura Carver for cheaper for the same size screen and unlimited storage (but you won't get a touchscreen or ability to rotate between portrait and landscape modes, which the Nixplay Classic can do).

Skylight Frame 2 for $190: Skylight's photo frames are where the organization originated, but I do prefer its calendars over its photo frames. The Frame 2 is its latest generation, and the best part is that you can swap out the frames, which Skylight named Snap Frames (starting at $15), to match the style of your home. You can upload photos by app or email, but you will need a subscription—Frame Plus, which costs $39 a year—to create albums, adjust settings using the app, upload videos, and add captions. The subscription doesn't control your actual storage, and instead the Frame 2 has a limit of 16 GB of storage.

Aura Mason for $199: The big original favorite from Aura, with a solid frame and the ability to rotate between landscape and portrait mode. It's still a great frame, but Aura did say they're sunsetting the model, but it'll remain available until it's sold out. It's still available so far.

Azorpa 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $90: This slim frame works well and has a nice affordable price point, and it can be rotated. It also has its own dedicated app, unlike several affordable models that all use the same Frameo app. But the ratio is slimmer than smartphone photos, so I found myself needing to constantly recrop pictures or have an extra border along two of the sides. If you don't mind a border and want a really cheap frame, this one's solid.

Cozyla frames: Our staffers have tried a few digital photo frames from this brand, and one of its digital wall calendars. Photo quality was great and there were solid features like only showing photos that match the current orientation of the frame. Our reviewer found the app to be frustrating, however, and it comes preloaded with unnecessary art images.

Familink 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $200: Familink's frame works with or without an internet connection, thanks to its 4G SIM card. Someone will need to set up an account on the website or app (iOS, Android) so that family members can send photos (or even chats) to the frame. There was no slideshow feature when we tested it in 2024, but the screen still looked good.

It has been revealed that loop Family Frame for $200: This is a good option if you want to text photos to a display, instead of using an app or an email. It's a good convenient option to use with family members. It's a solid overall photo frame, and has a touchscreen.

Industry observers note that pexar 2K Digital Picture Frame by Lexar for $180: This frame can rotate to be either portrait or landscape mode, and has a little stand that attaches via magnet for either position. It's a fine frame, but the screen isn't as nice as those for a similar price. The Pexar is made by Lexar but uses a third-party app, Frameo, which works fine but has a weirdly Instagram-like uploader that's limited to 10 photos.

In a recent development, skylight 10-Inch Frame for $190: A previous honorable mention, this frame is still solid. We like other frames better for the price, including the fresh Skylight Frame 2 (especially with its Snap Frame accessories). There's both a 10-inch version (with only 8 GB of storage) and a 15-inch version (with 16 GB of storage).

Vieunite's Textura Digital Canvas for $754 (USD shown in cart): Beautiful for displaying professional art, this one is bright and high-def enough that you don't lose the integrity of the original painting. It's extremely expensive, though, even if it's cheaper than buying an actual van Gogh.

How Do Digital Photo Frames Work?

Digital photo frames collect your photos, usually through an app but also through email and sometimes text, and display them onto the digital screen. They're created to look like a real frame, but instead show off hundreds or thousands of photos without you needing to reframe anything or print every single picture. Our favorite picks all have an app with storage, so they use Wi-Fi to connect the photos to the frame, but some frames also have physical storage on the device to store and remember the pictures.

What Should You Look For In a Digital Photo Frame?

Here are the top features you should check in a frame:.

What Storage Options Are There on Digital Photo Frames?

According to recent reports, all the main frames we recommend use cloud-based storage, so you'll upload your photos to a cloud server for the frame to reach and display them. Aura has unlimited storage for photos, while Nixplay charges $30 a year for unlimited photo storage (along with other features). While both use cloud storage, these are both reputable companies with defined privacy and security practices. Some of the cheaper frames you'll find won't have these processes in place.

Sources indicate that some frames have internal storage that can be expanded with SD cards or even use a USB stick. These options can be more secure, especially if you're moving photos yourself from the computer to the USB or SD card and then connecting it to the frame, but it’s also more work.

Do Smart Displays Work as Digital Photo Frames?

If you already have a smart display, you can set it to cycle through your photo albums when it's idle. The best one for this by far is the Google Nest Max ($230), though the Apple HomeView is another option I'm considering for this guide. It uses Google Photos to pull pictures, so if you're already a Google Photos user, it's an easy transition. But even if you aren't, adding your pictures to Google Photos is much, much easier than using Amazon's uploading tool in the Alexa app if you're using an Echo Show display, though you can also use the Amazon Photos app that works similar to the Google Photos app. You'll use that app for the Alexa Photo Frame I recommend above.

How Does Privacy and Security Come Into Play With Digital Photo Frames?

You might not think that photos count as sensitive information, compared to a bank account statement or your Social Security number. But it can be devastating to find photos of loved ones used for nefarious or unsavory purposes.

This is why we prefer frames from reputable companies like Aura and Nixplay over cheaper ones with less clearly defined privacy and security practices. Nixplay offers reasonable security measures, like encrypting your photos during transmission, and Aura offers the option to delete metadata, like the location where a photo was captured. However, both say they may disclose personal information if court-ordered or subpoenaed, and neither provides safety guarantees against hacking.

If you're concerned about security, you can avoid connecting to third-party services, but your most secure option is to just download several photos on a tablet and disable all internet connectivity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ll soon be able to watch video podcasts through the Apple TV app.

Apple is making a bigger push into video podcasts by adding a dedicated section for them to the Apple TV app. Apple prepares to increase the number of video podcasts that are available through the Podcasts app as well.

According to recent reports, developers will be able to check out the video podcasts section on Apple TV starting today before Apple makes it available to everyone. The section, which won't be locked behind a subscription, will be accessible on Apple's own set-top box, iPhone, iPad, Mac and CarPlay-enabled vehicles, as well as on the Apple TV app on third-party devices. (HomeView seems like a natural fit for video podcasts, but Apple didn't explicitly say whether they'll be available on the Apple TV app on that device.).

According to recent reports, "We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens," Oliver Schusser, an Apple vice president whose portfolio includes Apple TV and podcasts, told The Upcoming York Times. "It's really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn't approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.".

Like with just about everything these days though, Apple's push into video podcasts is part of a battle for consumers' attention. While the company helped popularize podcasts in the 2000s with the iPod, the company hasn't kept up with Spotify, YouTube and Netflix as video versions of shows became more prevalent. Earlier this year, Apple brought its HTTP Live Streaming video protocol to the Podcasts app, allowing users to switch between watching and listening to shows. The company told the Times that, in a given month, over 35 percent of video podcasts users switch between watching and listening.

Serena Williams and longtime business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures.

The firm is seeking to raise $200 million in capital to back AI-native companies that are “solving critical, underserved problems for individuals across the experience economy,” including in areas such as fintech and health and wellness, the fund stated in a press release announcing its launch.

This fund is separate from Serena Ventures, which Williams founded in 2022. A rep for Starfire confirmed that Serena Ventures has recently cut its last check, though a team remains to support the existing portfolio. Serena Ventures backed more than 100 companies and raised over $100 million in capital. Ferreira worked as an advisor and general partner at Serena Ventures and has co-invested with Williams since 2015 when they backed MasterClass’ seed round.

This newly introduced firm, Starfire, is a continuation of that business partnership, with Williams saying in the press release that it was “designed to live beyond” them and that the goal remains to broaden “access to capital” and create “opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”.

macOS 27.3 includes newly introduced privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last month, Apple revealed its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.
  • With today’s fresh macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.
  • In a post on its developer website last month, Apple remarked some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put consumers at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month, Apple revealed its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.

With today’s fresh macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple remarked some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put consumers at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple notes that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”.

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:.

For the latter, people will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for consumers to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Sources indicate that apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let customers know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Recent findings suggest that crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

According to recent reports, users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a latest support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

Apple states the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to revision their apps to account for situations where people grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for fresh installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

Tech Report: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that instagram revealed on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts.
  • While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app.
  • By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that instagram revealed on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content.

While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned firm told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio.

By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content.

Instagram claims adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees.

Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products.

When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL.

Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon.

The upcoming integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform.

Breaking: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August, Amazon revealed plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.
  • For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous.
  • The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August, Amazon revealed plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.

For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.

The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.

Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.

Recent findings suggest that drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.

Recent findings suggest that the first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.

Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.

It has been revealed that over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.

It has been revealed that israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:.

Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.

In a recent development, that experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”.

Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”.

In a recent development, “The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”.

Similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “.

The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.

Recent findings suggest that that anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”.

Industry observers note that the use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.

Sources indicate that according to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould said social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.

The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.

In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.

According to recent reports, the dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.

US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.

The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:.

It has been revealed that drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.

It has been revealed that while little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.

Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.

The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worlds level of dronophobia.

According to recent reports, over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.

In November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.

According to recent reports, around the same time, a rash of civilian “drone sightings” across the US emerged, particularly in Upcoming Jersey. Anxiety grew further after a Republican New Jersey congressman claimed there was an “Iranian drone mothership.” Segments of the population were ready to shoot down drones themselves.

Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to rapidly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.

PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.

I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

How to stream Twitch on your TV

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Twitch is one of the largest streaming platforms for gamers and content creators alike.
  • In a recent development, but before you go through the hassle of fishing out a Chromecast or a gaming console, make sure your TV doesn't already have Twitch as an available app.
  • In a recent development, twitch offers support for cross-device streaming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Casting Twitch to your TV has never been easier.

Twitch is one of the largest streaming platforms for gamers and content creators alike. Millions watch their favorite creators across PCs, laptops and mobile devices. It's the perfect platform for streaming on a larger screen, yet many TVs don't have Twitch built in. Thankfully, several methods let you stream Twitch to your television, from video casting to third-party streaming devices.

In a recent development, but before you go through the hassle of fishing out a Chromecast or a gaming console, make sure your TV doesn't already have Twitch as an available app. Most modern smart TVs have an app library where you can download apps like Twitch. If you haven't already, check your TV's app store to see whether you can install Twitch. If your TV doesn't have an app store, fret not. Casting your device to your television is a great alternative that nearly every TV supports, though you might need a streaming device to begin casting.

In a recent development, twitch offers support for cross-device streaming. You'll need a TV that supports streaming or a device that enables it, such as Google's TV Streamer. Casting to your television varies slightly depending on how you're using Twitch. If you're using the Twitch app on your mobile device, casting Twitch to your television is as easy as tapping the cast button on your favorite stream. If you don't see the option, make sure your phone and television are on the same Wi-Fi network and that both devices have the latest firmware. It's also worth checking your Twitch settings to ensure that you don't have any unwanted security settings, such as AI training, enabled.

According to recent reports, streaming Twitch from your computer is a little different but still fairly easy. Use Google Chrome as your web browser, since it lets you stream your screen to another device. Once you've loaded Twitch, click on the three dots on the top-right of your browser to bring up an options menu. Select the "Cast, Save and Share" ribbon and click on "Cast." Select your television to begin casting. As with the mobile device method, make sure your computer and television are set up on the same Wi-Fi network or the option won't appear. If casting the specific window doesn't work, you can also try casting your entire screen.

In a recent development, if casting content doesn't work, you can always use a streaming device. Gaming consoles are the best option here since most have a Twitch app you can install. Boot up the Twitch app from your preferred console and watch your favorite streams. Previous-generation and modern-gen PlayStation and Xbox consoles include a Twitch app; the Switch and Switch 2 do not.

Consoles aren't the only devices that can stream. You can also use an Amazon Fire Stick, a Roku device or Apple TV 4K to watch Twitch on your TV. The Fire Stick has an official Twitch app you can install; the Roku doesn't, but it does support casting and screen mirroring. If all else fails, you can also connect your laptop or desktop directly to your TV via HDMI or DisplayPort. Play Twitch on the connected device, then switch your TV's input to that device to enjoy the stream. Remember, you'll need to switch streams on the connected device, not on your TV.

Latest Update: Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, latest Harvard research has found.
  • The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.
  • Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, latest Harvard research has found.

The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.

Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public.

The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI.

“Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” notes Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study.

To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study.

In a recent development, “Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” notes Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.”.

In a recent development, while based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the latest study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers.

In a recent development, “Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.

Industry observers note that the study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent.

While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

What's a Grand Theft Auto game without a killer soundtrack?

From the sun-soaked synth-pop of Vice City to surfing a sea of radio stations, music has always been an essential part of Rockstar Games' gritty, open-world franchise. And with Grand Theft Auto VI taking players back to Vice City, the sprawling soundtrack is shaping up to be just as ambitious as the game itself.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been a busy year for Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao.

After closing a $65 billion funding round in May, he's been readying the artificial intelligence organization for what's widely expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering. The listing could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion, instantly making it one of the largest tech companies in the world.

Industry observers note that rao joined Anthropic in 2024, when the company was still considered an underdog to OpenAI, now its chief rival. He's known as a straight shooter and a deft operator with a relentless work ethic, according to Anthropic investors and former colleagues, and he's played a crucial role in fueling the company's historic rise.

It has been revealed that the 43-year-old finance chief has largely stayed out of the public eye, opting to yield the spotlight to Anthropic's seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei. But Anthropic's upcoming Nasdaq debut, which is expected to take place on Thursday, will likely push him to center stage, as public market investors and analysts hang on his every word for insight into the AI trade.

Rao has nearly two decades of experience in finance across a range of companies, including Fanatics Commerce, a sports merchandise retailer, Cedar, a healthcare payments and billing platform, Airbnb and Blackstone. But he's never taken a firm public as a CFO, and the stakes are high.

Investors are still reeling after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia following shocking reports of three extramarital affairs. The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates would make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.

Against that backdrop, Rao is under pressure to deliver.

In a recent development, "He's a committed professional. He's integrity-based, and he's had this meteoric rise in a very, very complex set of companies," Jonathan Mildenhall, Airbnb's former marketing chief and a Fanatics board member, told CNBC in an interview. "There was nothing easy about Airbnb. There was nothing easy about Fanatics. There's nothing easy about Anthropic, and yet he makes it look so.".

According to recent reports, CNBC spoke to current Anthropic investors, Rao's friends and former colleagues for this story, many of whom asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Rao declined to participate in an interview through an Anthropic spokesperson.

As Anthropic's first CFO, Rao has been instrumental in helping the manufacturer raise tens of billions of dollars over the past two years.

He has made himself easily accessible to Anthropic's backers, even during fast-moving, tense discussions about allocation sizes and valuations, according to investors. He often communicates in short bursts of texts or via quick phone calls, sometimes late into the night and through weekends.

Sources indicate that "He will communicate even bad news very directly, and I think that's key in this role, especially as they're launching into the public life," Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, a repeat Anthropic investor, told CNBC in an interview. "He doesn't let the important stuff go unsaid, and he's very good at giving you headlights into what's coming.".

Rao has a deep mastery of the nuts and bolts of Anthropic's business, as well as its broader strategy, and he's able to translate the complexities into language that financiers understand, according to investors and a former colleague. That's been especially useful ahead of the IPO, while Wall Street has been working to digest Anthropic's ambitious infrastructure plans, the people mentioned.

Anthropic has to secure massive amounts of computing power to train AI models and serve customers, and has entered into a range of purchase and lease agreements to try to meet anticipated demand. The company mentioned in an amended prospectus last week that its aggregate spend commitments total roughly $900 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.".

It has been revealed that "The compute that we procure, it's the lifeblood of our business," Rao said during a rare podcast appearance on "Invest Like The Best" in May. "It is the most important thing in the firm. It's like the canvas on which everything else gets built.".

Rao's frank communication style is different from that of Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, who's known for penning long essays and opining about AI's transformative potential and grave risks. But the pair complement one another well, according to investors, and Rao has earned Amodei's trust.

Recent findings suggest that both executives have been closely involved with Anthropic's fundraising efforts and IPO planning, but Rao has taken the lead in many of those discussions. He's been front and center during Anthropic's road show, and he led the early testing-the-waters meetings that the organization held in August, as CNBC previously reported.

Deeter called Rao "the glue" of the company, helping turn the founders' ideas into reality.

For friends and early colleagues, Rao's ascension hardly came as a surprise.

He earned his undergraduate degree in economics at Harvard University, where he graduated summa cum laude in 2005. Six years later, after a stint as a strategy consultant at Bain & Tech giant, he completed his J.D. at Yale Law School.

Recent findings suggest that instead of pursuing a career as a lawyer, Rao took a job at Blackstone and worked as a private equity investor. He soaked up the training he received there and was regarded as a competent and personable teammate, according to a former colleague. Rao is also credited with inspiring the private equity unit's annual poker tournament, after he famously schooled his bosses during a game in 2014.

The following year, Rao followed Blackstone's then CFO, Laurence Tosi, to Airbnb, where he cut his teeth in the world of fast-growing tech startups.

Rao helped lead the financing that kept Airbnb afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic, which he's publicly described as a "harrowing time" for the business. During his May podcast appearance, Rao stated Airbnb lost 70% of its revenue during a seven-week period. The tech giant survived, and Rao helped support its IPO in late 2020.

In a recent development, "Airbnb was so dynamic," noted Mildenhall, who is now the chief marketing officer at Rocket Companies. "I think that both his short time at Fanatics and his time at Airbnb really gave him close proximity to visionary founders that have a relentless frustration with the status quo.".

While Airbnb was one of the fastest-moving startups of the 2010s, it would be dwarfed by the hypergrowth that Rao would later be tasked with steering at Anthropic.

Sources indicate that anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. In 2024, the year that Rao joined the organization, Anthropic generated a total of $386 million in revenue.

The tech giant could net more than $60 billion in proceeds through its IPO this week, as CNBC previously reported, and Rao will be charged with deploying that capital and ushering Anthropic into its next phase of life as a public company. As he prepares to dive headfirst into the world of quarterly earnings calls, investors and former colleagues said they believe he's up to the task.

Recent findings suggest that "What I do try to do, maybe once a week, is in a quiet moment, just think, 'Wow, this is really cool,'" Rao said in May. "'It's an incredible opportunity to work with this group of people on this problem at this manufacturer at this moment in time.'".
